title: Subxiphoid pericardial window
subtitle: Drainage and biopsy of the pericardium through an upper midline incision

sources.title: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases

indications: Symptomatic or recurrent pericardial effusion, especially malignant or purulent, or where tissue is needed for diagnosis.
Tamponade where needle pericardiocentesis is not possible or has failed (loculated, clotted or posterior effusion).
contraindications: Traumatic haemopericardium with ongoing bleeding (needs sternotomy or thoracotomy to control the source).
preparation: Echocardiography: size, location and loculation; signs of tamponade.
Plan the anaesthetic: induction can cause cardiovascular collapse in tamponade, so the patient is prepared and draped awake and the surgeon is scrubbed before induction.
Consent: bleeding, cardiac or coronary injury, recurrence, infection, and the possibility of sternotomy.
positioning: Supine with the head up about 30 degrees during induction; the chest and upper abdomen prepared before induction.
equipment: Basic laparotomy and sternotomy instruments available, a long scalpel, Allis forceps, suction, a large-bore drain, specimen pots and culture bottles, a sternal saw in the room.
anatomy: The xiphoid process and the linea alba, the diaphragm, the retrosternal fat, the inferior surface of the pericardium resting on the diaphragm, the right ventricle immediately behind it.
criticalSafety: Prep, drape and be ready to cut before induction in tamponade.
Open the pericardium under direct vision, grasping it so the heart falls away.
Know the plan and the person to call if the heart or a coronary vessel is injured.
commonErrors: Inducing anaesthesia before the surgeon is ready.
A blind stab into the pericardium.
Not sending fluid and tissue for diagnosis.
postop: Drain output charted; drain removed when it falls below the agreed threshold.
Echo before discharge or if symptoms return.
Follow up the cytology, microbiology and histology.

steps.emphasis: Anaesthetic plan for tamponade discussed; the surgeon scrubbed and ready before induction.
Supine, head up 30 degrees during induction.
Prep and drape the chest and upper abdomen before induction.
Pericardial fluid for cytology, microscopy and culture (including tuberculosis), and the excised pericardium for histology.
A single large drain into the pericardial space through a separate stab incision.
Close the linea alba carefully to limit incisional hernia.

step.pw.induction.title: Induction in tamponade with the surgeon ready
step.pw.induction.why: General anaesthesia and positive pressure ventilation reduce venous return; in tamponade this can stop the circulation. Being ready to decompress immediately is the safety net.
how: Monitor invasively before induction where possible.
Have the patient prepped and draped, and the surgeon scrubbed with the knife ready, before the anaesthetist induces.
Induce with drugs that preserve sympathetic tone; if the pressure falls, decompress at once.

step.pw.incision.title: Upper midline incision and excision of the xiphoid
step.pw.incision.why: The subxiphoid route reaches the inferior pericardium without opening the sternum or the pleura.
how: Make an upper midline incision over the xiphoid down to the linea alba, staying out of the peritoneum.
Excise or retract the xiphoid process.
Develop the plane behind the sternum bluntly with a finger, staying above the diaphragm.

step.pw.pericardium.title: Identifying and opening the pericardium
step.pw.pericardium.why: The pericardium is opened under direct vision so the fluid escapes and the heart falls away from the knife.
how: Identify the pericardium as a tense, smooth membrane; feel the heart beating behind it.
Grasp it with two Allis forceps and lift; open it between them with a knife or scissors.
Aspirate fluid and send samples; watch the blood pressure rise as tamponade is relieved.
pitfalls: Draining too fast in a patient with longstanding effusion (decompression syndrome).

step.pw.window.title: Creating the window and exploring
step.pw.window.why: Excising a piece of pericardium both prevents early closure and provides tissue for diagnosis.
how: Excise a piece of pericardium about 3 to 4 cm across.
Break down loculations gently with a finger; inspect the visible pericardium for tumour or exudate.
pitfalls: Aggressive finger dissection over the right ventricle.

step.pw.bailout.title: Bailout: cardiac or coronary injury
step.pw.bailout.why: A tear in the right ventricle or a coronary vessel bleeds massively; the window does not give enough access to repair it.
how: Press a finger on the bleeding point; tell the anaesthetist and call for a cardiac surgeon and blood.
Extend to a sternotomy if trained and equipped, or keep pressure until help arrives.
Do not place blind sutures through the right ventricle near a coronary artery.
pitfalls: Blind suturing through a small window.
